newsitem.title: USA: Risks and opportunities in new funds.
newsitem.headline: Risks and opportunities in new funds.

text.p: Should you buy a brand new mutual fund? The very question provokes dismay among some fund industry observers, who argue that buying a fund without a track record is extremely dangerous.

They might be right. But there is at least one reason to consider adding some new blood to your fund portfolio: Many new funds in recent years have posted very impressive returns. Several recent studies have found that over the past decade, new funds have generated above-average returns during their first year of existence.
It's not hard to understand why new funds perform well. The main reason: New funds are small.

These days, the most successful funds get big quickly, as investors scramble to buy their shares. But that very success breeds failure: Managers of big funds have a hard time finding enough good stock picks to put all of their cash to work. They end up throwing some of the money at stocks that would never have made the cut in the early days of the fund. Result: Mediocrity, in many cases.

By contrast, new funds typically have small asset bases. Thus, the fund's managers can pour all of their money into a few of their favourite ideas. Assuming that the manager is a reasonably good stock picker, that can benefit the fund's performance.

At the same time, a small fund can be far more nimble when it buys or sells. For example, if a giant fund with $4 billion in assets wants to invest 1 percent of its holdings in a particular stock, it must buy $40 million worth. Clearly, the manager can't go out and buy it all at once. If he tried, he'd send the stock price skyrocketing before he could finish buying. So he must take days or even weeks to accumulate that position and, by then, the stock might not be cheap anymore. The problem is even greater when a big fund tries to invest in a small firm's shares.
Reason: A big fund has to buy a substantial portion of a small company's shares to make any noticeable mark on the fund's portfolio.

Likewise, a big fund might have trouble selling its position in a stock or an industry. Even a hint that a big fund is selling, say, technology stocks, could cause those stocks to slide. As a result, the fund could suffer big losses in that sector before it has a chance to finish selling.

By contrast, a new, small fund can zoom in and out of different stocks and sectors, guerrilla style, without exciting comment or affecting share prices. It can buy even the tiniest stocks, which may offer excellent bargains because the big funds can't buy them.

That said, there still are reasons to be leery of new funds as a group. For starters, they don't have track records. That makes it hard to predict how they might perform in various market environments.
Solution: Stick with new funds whose managers have established track records at other funds.

One promising candidate is Third Avenue Small-Cap Value (800-443-1021; $1,000 minimum investment; no load). Although the fund has existed only since April 1997, fund manager Marty Whitman is a veteran value hunter. His Third Avenue Value Fund has gained an impressive 21.3 percent annually during the past five years, versus 12.6 percent for its typical competitor. Third Avenue Small-Cap Value will invest in companies with market capitalisations of less than $1 billion. Whitman and co-manager Curtis Jensen also look for stocks that trade for at least 50 percent below their private market value. The fund's top two holdings recently were Nissan Marine & Fire, a Japanese property and casualty company, and FSI International, Inc., a semiconductor and equipment manufacturer.

A three-month-old fund with potential is Yacktman Focused (800-525-8258; $2,500 minimum; no load). Manager Don Yacktman has led his more seasoned Yacktman Fund to a 26.9 percent annualized return during the past three years, versus 22 percent for similar funds. Moreover, the fund has been only about 40 percent as volatile as its typical peer during that time. The Yacktman Focused Fund takes Yacktman's best ideas and focuses them into a concentrated portfolio of approximately 15 issues. The fund's objective is to purchase shares of superior companies when those shares are trading at substantial discounts to their private market value.

A third fund worth considering is Robertson Stephens Diversified Growth (800-766-3863; $5,000 minimum; no load), which invests in small and medium-size firms. Since its inception in August 1996, the fund has posted a cumulative return of 33.1 percent, versus 21.5 percent for its typical peer. Manager John Wallace ran Oppenheimer Main Street Income & Growth from 1991 to 1995. During that time, the fund gained 31 percent annually, approximately twice the return of the S&P 500.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers financial issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
